name: Thematic Coding
title: Thematic Coding
answer: Thematic coding is the qualitative research practice of sorting segments of text, transcript, image or field note into named categories so that patterns across a corpus can be described and compared. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where it supplies the interpretive layer that counts and models cannot produce on their own. The unit of work is the code, a short label attached to a passage, and the themes that emerge when codes are grouped and related. It is used in interview studies, focus groups, open survey responses, document review and ethnographic fieldwork.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Thematic coding is the qualitative research practice of sorting segments of text, transcript, image or field note into named categories so that patterns across a corpus can be described and compared. It sits inside qualitative analysis and mixed methods, where it supplies the interpretive layer that counts and models cannot produce on their own. The unit of work is the code, a short label attached to a passage, and the themes that emerge when codes are grouped and related. It is used in interview studies, focus groups, open survey responses, document review and ethnographic fieldwork.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a corpus of source material, a codebook or coding frame, and a system for storing and retrieving coded segments. That system may be a qualitative data analysis package, a spreadsheet, or a shared document, and increasingly it includes a language model that suggests candidate codes or clusters passages. Whatever the tooling, the corpus and the codebook remain the load-bearing parts, because a code means nothing without the passage it was attached to and the definition that governed its use. Version control matters as much here as in software, since a codebook that changes silently makes earlier coding unreproducible.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Coding usually proceeds through repeated reading, open coding of first passages, comparison of codes across cases, and consolidation into a smaller set of themes with written definitions and example quotations. Two or more coders often code an overlapping subset independently, then meet to resolve disagreements and refine the frame, which is how reliability is estimated. Machine assistance is now common at the suggestion and clustering stage, but the interpretive decision about what a passage means stays with the researcher. Auditability comes from keeping a trail of code definitions, memos, and the reasoning behind merges and splits.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main obligations are consent, confidentiality and the handling of identifiable material, since transcripts frequently contain names, workplaces and health details that a code label does not remove. Provenance matters when a model has been used to propose codes, because a reader needs to know which labels came from a person and which from a system, and on what text the system was run. Where published work is cited, this site links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, so a reader can check the source directly. Copyright and licence terms also apply to any corpus of documents that was not collected by the researcher.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward hybrid workflows in which models handle the mechanical parts of sorting and retrieval while researchers own the interpretive claims, with more attention paid to documenting that division of labour. Expect growing interest in codebook transparency, in reporting how much of a coding frame was machine suggested, and in methods for testing whether a theme holds across subsets of a corpus. The library here, with 319 research papers and 14104 extracted claims, reflects how quickly the methodological literature around these questions is accumulating.
